title: A migration guide for your own customers
metaTitle: A migration guide customers can use
excerpt: If customers must move, give them the order of steps, what will break, and how long it takes. A cheerful announcement can link to that guide. It cannot replace the steps.
alt: A silver laptop open to a code editor on a white desk, with a monitor, mug, and phone behind it, the working surface a customer needs when they have to move.
caption: A laptop, a monitor, and a mug. A migration guide is the order of steps, not an announcement. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What does a customer migration guide have to include?
faqs.answer: The steps in the order the customer must do them, a way to know each step worked, what will break or not come across, and how long the move takes. Name which steps are yours and which are theirs. An announcement without those facts is not a guide.

faqs.question: How should you describe the time a migration takes?
faqs.answer: Give a range you have observed, and say what it assumes, such as the size of the catalog. Include waiting time, like an overnight copy, not only the minutes of clicking. If your last moves took a day, the guide should say a day.

faqs.question: Where should the steps live?
faqs.answer: On a page you can correct when a button changes, linked from the announcement and from the product. A PDF emailed once will be wrong for later customers, and you will not know who still has it. Put known errors next to the step they belong to.

markdown:
A migration guide tells a customer how to move, in order, including what will break and how long the move takes. A product migration guide ux is that sequence, written for the person who has to do it on a Tuesday, not for the person who announced it. A cheerful announcement is not a guide. It can link to the guide. It cannot replace the steps.

If you do not yet know the order, what breaks, or the time, you are not ready to ask customers to move. Learn those three, then write.

## The order of steps, and nothing else first

Open with the outcome and the time. "Moving the catalog takes most teams one working day. Orders already placed stay on the old system until they ship." Then the steps, numbered, in the order a person must do them. Not the order your team built them. The order of dependencies.

Each step is a verb, a place in the product, and a way to know it worked. "Export the customer list from Settings, then upload it on the new account. You are done with this step when the count matches." A step without a check is how people get halfway and freeze.

Say which steps are yours and which are theirs. "We copy the files on Friday night. You re-invite your staff on Monday." Shared work with no owner is where migrations stall and tempers rise. Name the owner in the step.

Keep the path short enough to finish. If you have twenty steps, group them into phases the person can pause between. Preparation. The move. The morning after. People can hold a phase. They cannot hold a wall of bullets that all look equally urgent.

Google's helpful-content guidance asks whether a reader leaves able to achieve a goal. This page has one goal: complete the move without guessing. If they still need a call to learn the order, the guide is a brochure. Offer the call as help, not as the only place the steps exist.

Write the steps in the product's words. The button says "Export." The guide says "Export." A synonym you liked better in the draft will be wrong on the day, when they are looking at the screen and your sentence does not match it. Got Next and Leadly, as public product interfaces, live or die by that match between word and control. A migration guide is a script for those controls.

## What breaks, said before it breaks

List what will stop working, for how long, and what will not come across. Drafts that were never saved. Integrations you do not carry forward. Reports that will look different. Links that will change. The old mobile app, if the new one replaces it.

Say what is safe. Orders in flight. Paid invoices. The thing they are most afraid of losing. If you cannot say it is safe, say what you will do about it. "We export a copy you can download for ninety days" is a plan. "Don't worry" is not a plan.

Be specific about the ugly cases. A half-finished record. A user who never accepted the old invite. A file name with a character your new system rejects. These cases are the support queue. Meeting them in the guide is cheaper, and it is kinder. If you do not know the ugly cases, run the migration with one real customer and write down what broke. That customer is your editor.

Down the Cove, a public Hanabi project, was an ecommerce migration and redesign. The lesson for a guide is the shopper and the merchant both need to know what changed. A customer-facing guide and an internal runbook are different documents. Do not publish the runbook. Do publish the parts a customer must do, and the parts they will notice.

If something irreversible happens at a step, say so before the button. "Deleting the old connection cannot be undone. Download the file first." Put that sentence in the product too, not only in the guide. A guide that warns, and a button that does not, is a trap you documented.

## How long it takes

Give a range a normal customer can plan around, and say what the range assumes. "Under an hour for a catalog of a few hundred items. A day if you are matching old categories by hand." If the time depends on them, say which step burns the time.

Give the clock time as well as the effort time when there is a wait. "The copy runs overnight. You will have access at 8 a.m. your warehouse time." A spinner with no clock is how someone stays up for no reason. If you cannot name the hour, do not start the migration that night.

Say what they should not schedule against the move. A sale, a payroll, a campaign send. You know the collisions better than they do. One sentence of warning is part of the design. It is not pessimism.

Do not publish a duration you hope for and call it typical. Support will inherit the gap. If your last ten migrations took a day, the guide says a day. Hope can live in your internal goals. The guide lives with the customer.

Update the range when the product gets faster. A guide that still says "allow a week" after you automated the import trains people to delay a move they could finish after lunch. Stale fear is still stale.

## The announcement is a different page

The announcement says what is changing, when, and why they should care. It links to the guide. It does not contain the only copy of step four. People will need the steps again, on the day, and they will not find them inside a newsletter from last month.

Lead the announcement with the customer's outcome, then the date, then the link. "You can export the month without the old workaround, starting 4 May. The move takes about an hour. Here is the guide." A banner in the product can repeat that, with the date, until the date passes. Then take the banner down. An expired banner is how a product starts to look unattended.

Give them a backwards path if one exists. "You can stay on the current export until 1 June." A date with no path is a threat. A date with a path is a plan. If there is no backwards path, say that early enough that a customer can complain while you can still change the plan. Surprise is not a migration strategy.

Identify the audience of each sentence. Admins get the steps. Everyday users get what will look different on Monday morning. One guide can have both sections, clearly marked. A single voice that mixes "click Export" and "your team may notice a new color" will be skimmed past by both groups.

Hanabi would design the guide as a page in the product's information architecture, not as a PDF frozen in a slide. A page can be fixed when step three changes. A PDF emailed once will be the wrong instructions for half the customers, and you will not know which half. The site stack, Next.js and a content model a person can edit, matters here only because someone must be able to correct a step without a release panic. The client portal, on a Hanabi project, is where the longer notes live after delivery. Your customers need the short version in the product.

## Try the guide before you send it

Run the migration yourself with the guide open and nothing else. No internal runbook on the second monitor. Every time you have to ask a colleague what a step meant, the step is wrong. Fix the sentence, then run it again. A guide that only works for the person who wrote it is a diary.

Do this on a phone if any of your customers will. Warehouse leads and shop owners often will. A step that says "click the small arrow at the right of the toolbar" fails on a narrow screen if the toolbar has collapsed. Describe the control by its name. The WCAG principle of understandable content is the same idea: the instruction has to be operable where the work actually happens, not only on the designer's laptop.

Time the run. If you wrote "about an hour" and it took you three, change the guide before a customer inherits your optimism. Include the wait. A copy that runs overnight is not an hour of effort plus a shrug. It is a clock time they must plan. Write the clock time you just observed, with the assumption that made it true, such as the size of the sample catalog.

Ask one customer who is good at complaining to try a staging move. Pay them in attention. The sentences they stumble on are the sentences everyone else would have suffered in silence, then filed as tickets. Edit those sentences in the page, not in a follow-up email only they will see. The next customer deserves the corrected step.

## The morning after

End the guide with what done looks like, and what to check. The count of records. A sample order. A login from a second user. Three checks beat a paragraph of reassurance.

Say how to get help, and what you will ask. A screenshot, the step they were on, the time. A help path that starts with "just reach out" will produce unstructured panic. A path that asks for the step number will produce a fix.

Write the known errors next to the steps they belong to, not in a graveyard at the bottom. "If the count is short, you skipped archived customers. Go back to step two and include them." That is a guide. A troubleshooting appendix nobody opens is a second document.

Leave a way to know the migration happened. A date in the account. A note in the activity list. The person who did the work may not be the person who answers questions next month. The product should remember so the guide does not have to.

When the move is over, tell them what they can do now that they could not do before. That sentence is the release note. It should not be the only thing you sent them at the start. The piece on [release notes a customer will read](/blog/release-notes-a-customer-will-read) is the next read, so the announcement of the new capability stays as plain as the steps were.

For the shape of a studio that writes the path and then builds it, see [Hanabi's services](https://tryhanabi.com/#services). A migration guide is a product surface. It deserves the same care as the screen it points at.
